## For Loops {#sec-loops .core}

[**Core**]{.core-text}

[↑ top](#)

A loop is a way of repeating a task multiple times in a computer program. 

There are two main types of loop, a **for loop**, which runs once for every item in a vector (or other sequence), or a **while loop** which runs until a certain condition is met. 

In these practicals we will focus on **for loops**, which perform a task a fixed number of times or once for each item in a sequence.

We usually loop over a vector, meaning we perform the task once for each item in the vector.

To repeat a task `n` times, we can use `seq_len(n)`. This creates a sequence from `1` to `n`. The loop then runs `n` times, once for each number in this sequence. If we run our loop as `for (i in seq_len(n))`, each time we pass through the loop, the value of `i` increases by one.

::: {.callout-note}
We can also use the syntax `1:n` to iterate through the numbers from 1 to `n`. We will always use `seq_len(n)` in these practicals, but you may see this alternative elsewhere.
:::

We refer to each pass through the loop as an **iteration** - we **iterate** over a loop.

In a loop we use curly brackets `{}` to show which code is part of the loop - so everything inside the brackets will be repeated every time we iterate through the loop.

For example:

```{r for_loop_n}
for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  print(i)
}
```

We can add steps to our loop to run on each iteration.

```{r for_loop_complex_n}
for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  # add 2 to i
  j <- i + 2
  # take the square root of j
  sj <- sqrt(j)
  # round sj to the nearest whole number
  rsj <- round(sj)
  # print rsj
  print(rsj)
}
```

We can use our variable `i` inside the loop but we don't have to, we can just use it to set the number of iterations.

::: {.callout-exercise #ex-loops_1 .core}

### For loops

[**Core**]{.core-text}

In your `prac3_exercises.qmd` quarto document, generate two for loops:

1. A `for` loop which calculates and prints the **cube** of each number from 1 to 20.

::: {.callout-note #note-powers}

The operator `^` is used for powers in R, so e.g. 2^2 is 2 squared, 4^12 is 4 to the power of 12.

:::

2. This code snippet generates a random 5 letter character string.

`paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse="")`

Using a `for` loop, generate 5 such strings.

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-loops_1_ans}

[A `for` loop which calculates and prints the **cube** of each number from 1 to 20.]{.blue-text}

```{r loops_1_ans}
for (i in seq_len(20)) {
  print(i^3)
}
```

[This code snippet generates a random 5 letter character string: `paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse="")`. Using a `for` loop, generate 5 such strings.]{.blue-text}

```{r loops_2_ans}
for (i in seq_len(5)) {
  print(paste(sample(letters, 5, replace = TRUE), collapse = ""))
}
```

:::
:::

You can also use a for loop to do something to each item in a vector.

For example, in the below, we loop through the animals in our vector `species`. Inside the loop, the value of the variable `spp` changes on each iteration.

The cowsay package uses the `say()` function and the argument <code>by = [animal_name]{.orange-text}</code> (where [animal_name]{.orange-text} is the name of an animal) to print [ascii art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ASCII_art) of animals (and their associates) saying things.

```{r for_loop_vector}
library(cowsay)
species <- c("frog", "stegosaurus", "squirrel", "ghost")

for (spp in species) {
  say(paste("I am a", spp), by = spp)
}
```
As before, you can add as many steps as you like to perform during each iteration.

Here, we check if each "species" name starts with the letter `s`.

```{r for_loop_vector_complex}
species <- c("monkey", "shark", "turkey", "snowman")

for (spp in species) {
  has_s <- startsWith(spp, "s")
  say(paste("Do I start with an s?", has_s), by = spp)
}
```

Remember that everything inside the brackets is part of the loop, everything outside the brackets is not.

For example, let's write a short story about bird migration, based on what we learned in practical 2.

The `cat()` function works like `print()`, but doesn't print each output on a new line.

```{r bird_story, results="hold"}
cat("A bird leaves west Africa.\n")

for (i in seq_len(25)) {
  cat("flap ")
}

cat("The bird arrives in Europe\n")
cat("6 months later...\n")
cat("A bird leaves Europe\n")

for (i in seq_len(100)) {
  cat("flap ")
}
cat("\nThe bird arrives in west Africa.")
```

Everything inside the brackets is repeated, everything outside of the brackets is not.

## Storing results from loops {#sec-storing_results .core}

[**Core**]{.core-text}

[↑ top](#)

We sometimes want to store the results of running our loop in a vector or data frame.

For example, here we store all of the cubed numbers from our example above in a vector called `cubed_nums`. Before we start the loop, we create an empty vector using `c()`. Then, each time we pass through the loop, we use `c()` again to append the new result to the end of the vector. Once the loop has finished, `cubed_nums` contains the results from every iteration.

```{r store_cubes_vec}
cubed_nums <- c()

for (i in seq_len(20)) {
  res <- i^3
  cubed_nums <- c(cubed_nums, res)
}

print(cubed_nums)
```

We can also store the results of each iteration of a loop in a data frame.

One way to do this is to create an empty data frame before starting the loop using `tibble()`. During each iteration, we create a new one-row data frame containing the results from that iteration, then add it to the results data frame using the function `bind_rows()`.

`bind_rows()` combines two data frames row-wise — that is, it adds the rows of one data frame underneath the rows of the other. If the data frames do not contain exactly the same columns, the resulting data frame contains all columns present in either data frame, with `NA` used where a row has no value for a particular column.

![`bind_rows()` and `bind_cols()`](images/rbind_cbind.png){#fig-bind width="100%"}

In this case, each time the loop runs, `current_row` is replaced with the results for the current species, then `species_df` grows by one row.

For example, we can adapt our animal loop above to store both the species name and whether it starts with "s":


```{r bind_rows}
species <- c("monkey", "shark", "turkey", "snowman")
species_df <- tibble()

for (spp in species) {
  has_s <- startsWith(spp, "s")
  current_row <- tibble(
    Species = spp,
    Starts_with_S = has_s
  )
  species_df <- species_df |> bind_rows(current_row)
}
gt(species_df)
```

::: {.callout-exercise #ex-loop_df .core}

### Build a 10-course breakfast

[**Core**]{.core-text}

The function `sample()` can select as single item from a vector.

For example:

```{r sample_animals}
breakfast <- c("eggs", "bacon", "sausages", "toast")
print(sample(breakfast, size = 1))
```
In your `prac3_exercises.qmd` Quarto document, using a `for` loop with 10 iterations, build a random 10-course breakfast. In each iteration:

* Choosing a random breakfast food from the vector above (or a vector of your choice)
* Choosing a random number between 1 and 5, to represent the number of that item you will have.
* Store the item and the number in a one-row data frame.
* Add this row to a data frame containing your complete breakfast

After this is complete, display your data frame.

::: {#copy-libraries .callout-note .copycode}
### Include this code

You will need to include the following as an R code chunk at the start of the document.

```{r libraries_visex, eval=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
```
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-loop_df_ans}

```{r loop_df_ans}
breakfast <- c("eggs", "bacon", "sausages", "toast")
nums <- seq_len(5)

break_df <- tibble()

for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  item <- sample(breakfast, size = 1)
  num <- sample(nums, size = 1)
  row <- tibble(
    item = item,
    count = num
  )
  break_df <- bind_rows(break_df, row)
}
gt(break_df)
```

:::
:::

## Review {#sec-summary_0301}

[↑ top](#)

::: {.callout-note #note-summary_0301}

### Programming summary

* A `for` loop repeats a task a fixed number of times.
* Each cycle through a loop is called an **iteration**.
* You usually use a vector to determine the iterations of the loop.
* You can store the results of your loop by adding to a vector in each iteration.
* You can also store the results by adding a new row to a data frame in each iteration using `bind_rows()`.
:::
